searchText: <maxwellfoley3> hey guys, this might be a noob question but ive been following the eth2 research and i want to make sure my understanding is correct. with this latest update where the shard count has been reduced to 64 and each beacon chain block contains the latest block of every shard, does this remove the need for developers to worry about asynchronous connections between shards (eg "yanking" and all that?) Or do these asynchronous interactions still need to be taken into account, its just that the overall experience will be much faster now? **will_vill** Cross shard communication will still need to be asynchronous, but now it can typically happen within one block vs. waiting for finality. <maxwellfoley3> what if you call a function thats like: do something in shard A => do something in shard B => return a value back to shard A? Would that take multiple blocks? <maxwellfoley3> intuitively it feels like a shard A validator wouldnt be able to do something in shard A, wait for a bit, then run more code in shard A within the same block **will_vill** Yes it would - and for the most part, HLLs like solidity should be able to abstract a lot of this into basic async programming models/calls <maxwellfoley3> ok cool thanks. makes sense **ajsutton** In the 0.9 spec, the deposit contract has a new depost data root param for the deposit function. The vyper code looks to be doing the same kind of merkelization as hash_tree_root or signing_root do, but neither of those actually match what the contract expects. Should it be the same as one of those or is the docs on what it should be somewhere? **ajsutton** Addendum: the deposit data root the contract accepts appears to be the same merkelisation as hash_tree_root but with the values for pubkey, withdrawal_credentials and signature reversed. So I suspect it should be the same as hash_tree_root and our implementation of that is using the wrong endianess. Would be very helpful if someone could confirm that though. depositors provide the expected leaf value as a checksum of sorts https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/issues/1357 this value is the hash tree root of a `DepositData` instance **ajsutton** Awesome thanks. So we have a big somewhere but since we’re passing the ssz ref tests which seem to check the hash tree root, it’s not there. I guess I’ll go play with some other clients and see what they think of my deposits... the fields appear to be in the correct order to me and i'm not sure how endianness plays a role **ralexstokes** @ajsutton worth spot checking one of the failures to make sure the hash tree root is what is differing, i’d wager **ralexstokes** im not sure if there are any tests yet covering this checksum bit wrt the deposit contract — someone else in this channel may know... **ajsutton** The deposit contract definitely doesn’t have tests but the ssz ones do cover it. The deposit contract only works on the data you give it, so my guess is that we’re giving it reversed input and our listener is then reversing it again. If I also reverse the data when creating the root it gets the same answer. So I think if all the reversing is just removed it will be right but will have to confirm that somehow. **ajsutton** I come to eth2 after all the endianness changing so don’t really know where the reversing came from. **ralexstokes** good luck 🙂 **ajsutton** Appreciate the help.

excerpts.author: eth2_gitter_bot
excerpts.content: <maxwellfoley3> hey guys, this might be a noob question but ive been following the eth2 research and i want to make sure my understanding is correct. with this latest update where the shard count has been reduced to 64 and each beacon chain block contains the latest block of every shard, does this remove the need for developers to worry about asynchronous connections between shards (eg "yanking" and all that?) Or do these asynchronous interactions still need to be taken into account, its just that the overall experience will be much faster now?

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**will_vill**
Cross shard communication will still need to be asynchronous, but now it can typically happen within one block vs. waiting for finality.

excerpts.author: eth2_gitter_bot
excerpts.content: <maxwellfoley3> what if you call a function thats like: do something in shard A => do something in shard B => return a value back to shard A? Would that take multiple blocks?

excerpts.author: eth2_gitter_bot
excerpts.content: <maxwellfoley3> intuitively it feels like a shard A validator wouldnt be able to do something in shard A, wait for a bit, then run more code in shard A within the same block

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**will_vill**
Yes it would - and for the most part, HLLs like solidity should be able to abstract a lot of this into basic async programming models/calls

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**ajsutton**
In the 0.9 spec, the deposit contract has a new depost data root param for the deposit function. The vyper code looks to be doing the same kind of merkelization as hash_tree_root or signing_root do, but neither of those actually match what the contract expects. Should it be the same as one of those or is the docs on what it should be somewhere?

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**ajsutton**
Addendum: the deposit data root the contract accepts appears to be the same merkelisation as hash_tree_root but with the values for pubkey, withdrawal_credentials and signature reversed. So I suspect it should be the same as hash_tree_root and our implementation of that is using the wrong endianess.  Would be very helpful if someone could confirm that though.

excerpts.author: ralexstokes
excerpts.content: depositors provide the expected leaf value as a checksum of sorts

excerpts.author: ralexstokes
excerpts.content: this value is the hash tree root of a `DepositData` instance

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**ajsutton**
Awesome thanks. So we have a big somewhere but since we’re passing the ssz ref tests which seem to check the hash tree root, it’s not there. I guess I’ll go play with some other clients and see what they think of my deposits...

excerpts.author: ralexstokes
excerpts.content: the fields appear to be in the correct order to me and i'm not sure how endianness plays a role

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**ralexstokes**
@ajsutton worth spot checking one of the failures to make sure the hash tree root is what is differing, i’d wager

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**ralexstokes**
im not sure if there are any tests yet covering this checksum bit wrt the deposit contract — someone else in this channel may know...

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**ajsutton**
The deposit contract definitely doesn’t have tests but the ssz ones do cover it. The deposit contract only works on the data you give it, so my guess is that we’re giving it reversed input and our listener is then reversing it again. If I also reverse the data when creating the root it gets the same answer. 

So I think if all the reversing is just removed it will be right but will have to confirm that somehow.

excerpts.author: eth2_bridge_bot
excerpts.content:
**ajsutton**
I come to eth2 after all the endianness changing so don’t really know where the reversing came from.
